The declarations in AppearanceAnimation.declarations.swift are recovered runtime
declarations, not a reimplementation. They belong inside the SwiftUICore module,
whose ABI name is SwiftUI. Compiling them as ordinary app Swift source would create
different symbols and is not supported.

Scripts/build-bridge.sh copies the selected local Apple SDK's public interface,
appends only AppearanceAnimationStrategy and appearanceAnimation, and compiles the
result with that Xcode toolchain. No system or SDK files are modified. The script
checks the SDK linker stub and links a probe against the actual system symbols.
It does not install, launch, or embed the probe in an app.

Do not distribute Generated/: it contains local Apple SDK interface copies and
compiler-specific artifacts. Rebuild it with the recipient's Xcode instead.

Generated output separates SDK_NAME and full target triple:
  Generated/iphonesimulator27.0/arm64-apple-ios26.0-simulator/Modules
  Generated/iphoneos27.0/arm64-apple-ios26.0/Modules
manifest.json records the original SDK interface hash, declarations hash, compiler,
and link result. Regenerate after changing Xcode or SDK, or changing the target's
deployment version. Each target needs the include path for its selected SDK and
deployment target; matching app and extension settings use the same generated path.

Runtime availability is separate from compilation. iOS 27.2 arm64 Simulator is the
only runtime tested in this investigation. A deployment target of 26.0 does not prove
these private functions exist or behave the same on iOS 26. Device compilation and
linkage, if performed, still do not establish successful execution on an iPhone.

No additional private framework, linker option, entitlement, or code-signing
exception is required by the tested Simulator implementation. Availability checks
for public iOS versions cannot establish private symbol existence on unknown OS
versions; use a compatible, explicitly validated runtime for this build.
